She used to go into homes and take care of babies when they were born. They didn't go to hospitals, and she used to do that and lots of times free of charge. But when she got older, she used to give free piano lessons to people that had many children in there. They were musical. She'd give her free lessons. Many times she did that. speaker: Monica Reller

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: And what was your father? What did your father do?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: My father was a blacksmith. And then he would, we alternated between farming and blacksmithing. So we moved. Three years or so the longest I ever remember living in a place until I got married. And, we've had, I had many farming experience. Like I said, I was the one he wanted to be a boy. And in North Dakota, when he used to hay, I had to be the one on top of the stack, or I had to run the moor or the buck rake. And we always lived quite a ways from school. We used to walk two or three miles to school, and when I went to high school, I started driving the car and I hadn't one lesson, and he gave me this car and told me to drive to. It must have been five miles. I had to go to town and I drove until it got cold and I froze the radiator. Then I had to walk to meet the bus and that was a couple miles. So North Dakota has a lot of memories for me. And I did the same year when we moved away.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Wow. Well, how many were in your family?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: There were four children. He had two children that had died after there was four. The three girls and there was a boy two years after myself. But just at the age when he got old enough to help, he had a ruptured appendix. And so he wasn't very well. And then when he got over that, then he went and worked out. And so I was the man around the house all my life. So.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: He was, he was out of the home?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: You know, then he'd go and work out by the people as soon as he got well over this ruptured appendix deal, and he never was back at home anymore. Well, my father worked out quite a bit, and we had a small farm, and it was during the Depression, and I can remember mother and I was home alone and we had our choice. We, in North Dakota, they always had a big night on Saturday night. Well, Mother's Day, well, we have our choice. We either have to spend this money that we get from the cows and the chickens to buy feed for them, or we can go out in the field because there wasn't very good standard for wheat. We can go out and cut the grain heads off and feed the chickens, and we'd spend that money, go to town Saturday night. So I did that. We herd the cattle. And then during those dust storms, I used to ride a horse and I would have to ride in a small meadow, and I have to ride constantly so that I could see the cattle. And I would take a book along to read. And before I could read one page, I had to brush or blow the dirt off the page so I could finish reading. It was that strong in the dirt. We used to, I would take a sack of, and a scissors. And over my back when I went out to herd the cattle, or put it on the horse and I go and cut off these wheat heads and take them home and feed the chickens so we could have our fun Saturday night.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: But, I love to make quilts. We have quilting every Tuesday, and we give them away to people that are poorer and burnouts. We give it to the kids that go away to school, or to young marrieds. And that's one of my cheap hobbies.

words: It's our church club and it's called. We call it the Community Services, and we have people in the community. Any time that you know anybody is in need, that's and we include any. But they don't have to be members of our church to come to the, so they help us with that.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, yeah. I go to a, Bible study group out on the ridge that I really enjoy, that there's some practically. Well, every church in town is included in this. And, no, it's the. But until then I'm going to play, so. But I think I'm at least 20 years older than any of the others that's coming. But I enjoy it.

speaker: Monica Reller

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson

words: And. Did you help, do you help your husband in his business?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, yeah. I go and drive cars, and I clean cars if necessary. I don't like to, but I will. And I do the office work here too. Besides, we have our house upstairs, and you can see that's a big elephant job. And then we have the greenhouse up behind. That last year was really good. Now everything's about dead and I'm just starting to get radishes up now.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Did, did you help to build this?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah. My only (unintelligible). Yeah, we built it ourselves mostly, except once in a while somebody that, yeah, I need to pay off a bill, they would help us. And once I think there was a carpenter that was out of work, and he said, he came to my husband, wanted to know if he could work. And he said, well, he give him so much an hour and he's always better and starting. So he really helped on that. And then there was a couple others came in and helped us when it was snowing, was putting on the roof, you know, we built it by sections. We only started with a little place and we were going to just be here in the daytime and look at the farm. And then I said, well, I want a room upstairs, because sometimes it's 10 or 11. So I wanted to have a place where I could rest. So the whole first year when we moved in, we climbed through a ladder through the main to this main place here. And then the next year we put the outside stairway on. And then we enclosed that. Now we're over there, 2 or 3 more sections. That's about as far as we'll go.

speaker: Monica Reller

And so she was sent to, over to Japan to one of our missionary colleges. And that's where she's teaching. And that's not where she met her husband, which is a teacher up there too, but he's a Japanese.

words: And, you have two other children?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: I have two boys and one boy lives across the land out there on the farm. He lives out in the country. He's got three sons, and he works kind of a carpet layer. And then he, (unintelligible) works here. You know, in between time, doing painting jobs, usually. On his own, he kind of works independently. And then the other boy runs the farm.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: (Unintelligible). Did you, have you held any other jobs?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, yeah. I've been a nurse, and I cooked at the university and.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: You cooked at one of the.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah. Sorority houses. When the Navy was here. Yeah.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: And then.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: That was mostly what I did. I've been, done mostly nursing.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Nursing. At Moscow or, around this area?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: No, in, just in Weiser, I haven't done any, well, just one job I took as a private, I worked at the bean. These sort of beans. At Wilford and Wilson. And then one of the boss's kids got sick, and then I went back and specialed that kid at home. And then I went to work for the university. I got this job at the university. I came out here. To then I've just been helping here on the farm and the orchard. We planted the orchard all ourselves. We raised a lot of oak trees from seed and did our own grafting and our own budding. In fact, we've done many things that the people in this area say is not possible. You know, take two limbs of apples and you wrap them together and they all make a tie. You can just walk right up the center of some of the trees. My son keeps cutting a lot. They don't like him, but that's what we get.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Do you feel like that you have more free time now than you did when you were younger? Or.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, I don't know what you mean by free time. I've always been busy doing something. I don't know, I feel kind of pressured because see we'd help with the farm, and then we're here at the car lot. So I think my time is pretty well spent. I mean, I don't have too much time that I can just say, well, okay, I'm just going to take off and do what I want.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: If you had a choice of. Did you, have you ever thought of what would happen if something happened to your husband? What you'd do?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, yeah, I wouldn't, I wouldn't run car lots, but. Oh, I think I'm old enough now. I'm getting awful close to retirement, and I've had a lot of hobbies. I'd just kind of keep on with my hobbies, I think. I don't think I'd really go out and look for work. I'm not too sure of that. If I did, I probably would maybe go in for. There is, a group that goes out and talks to the, you know, the blind or the deaf where they go and contact people like that. I wouldn't mind doing something like that, public service or something and, or maybe even into a restaurant. I could probably do something like that. I don't know, I used to think about it because I thought, well, I could go back into nursing, but, anymore, I think he'll outlive me.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: So it seems like that we went over the first part of your life pretty fast. Is there anything that you would like to add about how it was to get through the Depression? Or.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, the Depression. That's where I was saying that we cut off these heads and I was riding the cattle around, you know, to keep them, grazing. And because all the rest of the family was working except myself, I was home with my mother and we tended to everything there had to be done there on the farm. We didn't do any farming that year because of the dust. We just decided it wasn't worth it. So they all went to work and we just, went and volunteered, is what we had off the beat. And we just, I just turned the cattle and we just had chickens and cows, and, I can remember going to school and all the kids wore hand-me-down dresses. There was no fancy clothes. And then my older sisters graduated from high school, they, each one of the girls made their own dresses. They were all homemade dresses that year at the graduation. And, and I remember going that and that school where we was, it burned down and they built a new school. And when they built the new school, they put in a gym. They'd never had basketball there before. And I was still in the seventh and eighth grade when this came in. And I remember they came out with these shorts. And my dad, no girls of mine are ever going to wear those shorts, they're not going to play basketball. So the older girls, they never even turned out. But when I came out, I turned up and I got on the team and I played on the team all four years, and he didn't say a thing. In fact, he was proud of it. So. But I always learned how to work my folks. I you never I never learned to buck up. You know, I would just let things go and let things come on kind of gradually and I didn't have a problem. I didn't come right out and ask them either, though. See.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Okay.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: So I kind of worked that one over on the old man. But anyway, it was real fun. And the old school busses we used to drive, wasn't these fancy ones like you have now. It was just an old truck and they put an all wooden back on, and then had wooden seats on both sides, and they straddled everything down through the middle. And that's what they had for school busses, and we used to ride them. At, then I, we, my house, my folks was too far out and they imported the school teacher there, and her folks lived close. And so then I stayed at her home. So we just traded places, and I went in on their school bus and rode with their kids, it was quite piled in. And some mother kept a schoolteacher quite a few years that way. Yeah, we, we only lived a couple years out there, though. Then we moved to another place. I, I this year I want to go back and kind of look up some of those old places. They're having a reunion back at that school, and I want to go back and see if I can find some of these old friends of mine.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Oh. Oh, yeah. Well, could you, talk a little about how you've seen? You've lived here for 35 years, is that right?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: No, 32. Well, about 35 in Idaho probably.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Most of it in Troy, is that right?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: Okay. So, can you tell us something about some way how, Troy has changed in those 32 years?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, this, just the last couple years, it's kind of truly has grown. It was kind of a small place before, and, but now they're just really spreading out all over, you know, there's new houses in practically every area. And, ourselves, we can, we notice it more than we did before because we have an airplane and an airstrip right down the middle of the orchard we have out there.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: And when you get up and you can fly around, you can see the whole trailer houses and things moved in that wasn't there before, and a lot of people put in ponds. There's a lot of ponds in here that wasn't before. So I think that has changed our climate. I think that's made it warmer. We get more rain instead of snow.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: There, usually when they ask about our water shed, they always give us the Moscow. And we put in, we have five ponds on the place and my husband put it in himself. And of course I helped him. I used to run the roller and, and, we had to keep the rollers.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: The rollers?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah, he runs the bulldozer and pushes it. And then you have a roller with teeth on it to pack it. And I have done that. A couple of times, when we've made ponds around. In fact, like I said, we have the five ponds and when we put this big pond in, they come and said the roll, it'd take two years to fill it. And it was filled way before Christmas. Because, you see, we live close to the mountain, on that side mountain where the snow comes down, and we get about twice the rainfall than they do in Moscow. And they don't believe that. Until we fill that pond so fast. We can put it in a great big pond and we get, like I said, about twice the rainfall that Moscow gets, and snow too. And it's only all the water we get in our ponds is from rain and snow, and drainage from the hill and we put in a whole orchard. We have 60 acres of orchard up there that we planted ourselves. There was maybe a small cherry orchard at two different spots and a few apples when we got married. We tore down all the outbuildings like the barn and the chicken house and. Oh, we've had some very hair-raising experiences on that farm, and we was there, we moved the garage across and we was burning some, or, some of the lambs and stuff. And my husband pulled the garage right across there and set it over where we wanted to have it. And the oldest little boy was just about two years old, and he said, look, Daddy, pretty fire. Looked and the garage was on fire. There was a pretty fire on it. Loved it. Burned out the side of the garage. And then where, down where one pond is now, there was some big trees we were going to take out. And so one morning when the kids were in bed, we went out and put dynamite under these trees and, he had cut them off until they were fairly good sized stumps. And so we put them out and he said, let's run around behind the garage, you know, is when the dynamite was going to go up. And here that big stump came up and it came right down through the roof of the garage right there.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: And this is on your farm?

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Oh, it's on the farm out there. And there we stood and watched it, and it could have come right down through the bedroom just as easy. I remember the kids were sleeping. And another thing we did that everybody thought. My, my sister said, I'm going to write a book sometime about the crazy neighbors, and it's going to be about us. But, he was quite an inventor. We dug our basement with dynamite under the house, while the house was standing above it. He started in with a bulldozer on one side. And there's this heavy clay, you know, that you can't get into. So he just. He made a drill and he drilled so many holes and put dynamite in. But he got smarter, and he'd drill more holes and put them in. And he had just about cleared out when one time the first one went off before he got out. And he didn't think it was going to make it out of there, but. He had broken ribs. And I remember this clay, it came out and had really gotten him. We made it, we only broke one dish in that whole thing and shaken the house. So.

speaker: Monica Reller
words: So you really kind of contributed a lot. You, in being kind of a carpenter and a gardener and a farmer and a nurse and, you had quite a varied background.

speaker: Doris Burns Carlson
words: Yeah, very. And another thing that I think, too, that we hadn't quite done out in this vicinity is when the doctor came, he was the one that brought the skiing. And, the very first year he came, he put a ski tow up on the hill right above our house. And that's where we all learned to ski. All the children.

speaker: Monica Reller
